title: Pebble Duel star race and every start

families.title: Pebble Duel: star race and every start
families.mathematics: A token sits on a square board with a star in the bottom-left corner. A turn slides it straight left or straight down, one or more squares, and whoever moves it onto the star wins. A start is a second-player win exactly when every move from it leads to a first-player win, and working back from the star sorts every square. The square x columns right of the star and y rows up is two-pile Nim with piles x and y, so the second-player squares are the diagonal x = y: every move leaves it and every other square can return to it, which is the copying strategy. When the token may also slide diagonally down and to the left (a queen), each row, column and down-left diagonal holds at most one second-player square; they are Wythoff’s pairs (1, 2), (3, 5), (4, 7), (6, 10), … and their mirror images, (⌊kφ⌋, ⌊kφ²⌋) with differences 1, 2, 3, …. With three piles the second player wins exactly when every bundle size 1, 2, 4, … appears an even number of times across the piles (Bouton): a move always breaks a pair, and from an unpaired position one pile can be rebuilt to pair them all again.
rules: Players take turns. On a board, a turn slides the token straight left or straight down, one or more squares; on the queen boards it may also slide diagonally down and to the left. Whoever moves the token onto the star wins.
With piles, a turn takes one or more pebbles from one pile, and whoever takes the last pebble wins.
The app never misses a winning move.

puzzles.title: Four by four
puzzles.objective: Choose who starts, then move the token onto the star. Win 3 games in a row from new starts.
puzzles.instruction: Choose who starts, then move the token onto the star. Win 3 games in a row from new starts.
puzzles.controls: A turn slides the token straight left or straight down, one or more squares, and whoever moves it onto the star wins. Choose Me first or You first, then tap a dotted square to move the token there; I reply at once. Win 3 games in a row from new starts. After a loss, Same start again is practice and does not count.
rules: Players take turns.
A turn slides the token straight left or straight down, one or more squares.
Whoever moves the token onto the star wins.
Before each game, choose who starts. The app never misses a winning move.
Win 3 games in a row. Only games from a new start count; Same start again is for practice.
puzzles.idea: The starts where you would rather go second are the diagonal from the star.
puzzles.prerequisites: Take turns and slide a token along a row or a column. A grown-up can read the goal.
hints: Lost a game? Same start again replays that start. Watch where I move the token.
Starts where you went first and lost get a ring. What do they have in common?
When I won, where did my moves leave the token? No move goes from one of those squares to another.

parent.notice: Whether your child decides who starts by looking at where the token is, before playing, rather than by who won last time.
parent.prompt: From which squares would you rather go second? How can you tell?
parent.explanation: Square x columns right of the star and y rows up is the game with two piles x and y: a move left takes from one pile, a move down from the other. From a diagonal square (x = y) every move leaves the diagonal, and from any other square one move returns to it, so whoever moves the token onto the diagonal can keep it there (by copying) until it reaches the star. On this 4-by-4 board the 3 diagonal squares are the starts where you would rather go second. Starts are drawn half from them, and the app never misses a win, so three wins in a row from new starts shows the rule is known, not guessed.
parent.extension: Your partner goes first from the top-right corner. How can you always win?
parent.connection: The second-player squares are the P-positions of two-pile Nim, the equal pairs; copying is a strategy proved by an invariant (Ferguson, §1–2).

puzzles.provenance: Week 8 launch (a token on a 4-by-4 board) and K–1 Problems 1–2 (play many games from the dot; circle whether you would rather go first or second), as a choose-who-starts round on the Proofs duel engine.

puzzles.idea: With the diagonal move the diagonal is no longer safe; the second-player squares are 1 right 2 up, 2 right 1 up, 3 right 5 up and 5 right 3 up.
hints: Lost a game? Same start again replays that start. Watch where I move the token.

parent.prompt: From which squares would you rather go second? How can you tell?
parent.explanation: Work back from the star. Every square in the star’s row, column or diagonal is a first-player win (one move reaches the star). The nearest squares that cannot reach the star are 1 right 2 up and 2 right 1 up, and every move from them reaches a first-player win, so they are second-player squares. Each row, column and down-left diagonal can hold only one second-player square, since a move would join two of them. Continuing, the second-player squares on this 6-by-6 board are (1, 2) and (3, 5) and their mirror images. In general they are Wythoff’s pairs (⌊kφ⌋, ⌊kφ²⌋) and their mirror images, with φ the golden ratio; the k-th pair has difference k.
parent.extension: Why can no row hold two second-player squares?
parent.connection: Wythoff’s game (1907); its P-positions are (⌊kφ⌋, ⌊kφ²⌋) and their mirrors (Wythoff; Ferguson, §2 exercises).

parent.prompt: How do you know there is no other?

parent.notice: Whether your child finds the starts by organised search (fix the smallest pile) or by a pattern, and whether they notice that two piles fix the third.
parent.prompt: If two piles are 2 and 4, what must the third be?
parent.explanation: Write each pile in bundles of 4, 2 and 1. The second player wins exactly when each bundle size appears an even number of times (the Nim-sum is 0). For any two piles a and b the third must be a ⊕ b, so a start is decided by its two smallest piles; within 1 to 6 that gives 1, 2, 3; 1, 4, 5; 2, 4, 6; 3, 5, 6.
parent.extension: With piles up to 7, which three starts join these?
